items.title: Carbon pricing is the textbook fix for a textbook problem
items.claim: Climate change is often described as the largest market failure ever (Stern Review 2006). What's the standard economic prescription?

options.text: Pigouvian carbon pricing (tax or cap-and-trade) to internalise the social cost of carbon emissions; complementary policies for innovation, transition support and distributional fairness

items.reveal:
Arthur Pigou's 'Economics of Welfare' (1920) introduced taxes to internalise externalities. William Nordhaus's DICE model (1990s onwards) extended welfare economics to climate; he won the 2018 Nobel.

Real-world implementation: EU ETS (2005, world's largest cap-and-trade); UK Carbon Price Floor; Canada's federal carbon tax; California; Korea. Coverage and prices vary widely. As of 2023, ~25% of global emissions had a carbon price; average price below social cost estimates.

Distributional concerns and political economy of carbon pricing have limited adoption despite theoretical consensus.
items.why: Welfare economics provides a clear policy answer to climate change. Implementation is constrained by political economy more than by economic theory.

items.title: The impossible trinity constrains exchange rate policy
items.claim: Robert Mundell's impossible trinity (or trilemma) states that a country cannot simultaneously have:

options.text: A fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy. It must choose two of three

items.reveal:
Mundell's 1963 paper formalised the trilemma. Choices: fix exchange rate + free capital (give up monetary policy: e.g., classical gold standard, eurozone for individual members); free capital + monetary policy (give up fixed rate: US, UK, Japan); fix exchange rate + monetary policy (give up free capital: China, partly).

The ERM crisis (1992) and the Asian financial crisis (1997-98) both showed the cost of trying to maintain all three. Helene Rey's 2015 work argues that with global financial cycles, even floating exchange rates don't fully restore monetary independence — making the trilemma effectively a dilemma.
items.why: Exchange rate policy isn't a free choice; it's a constrained one. The trilemma sets the menu countries can choose from.

items.title: Switching costs create lock-in even without monopoly
items.claim: Mobile phone contracts, banking services and software subscriptions all create switching costs. How does this affect competition?

options.text: High switching costs reduce price elasticity, allow price discrimination, and create incumbency advantages; competition can shift from price-on-price to acquisition incentives that don't always benefit existing customers
Switching costs only exist in monopoly

items.reveal:
Klemperer's research (1987 onwards) formalised switching cost economics. UK's Open Banking initiative (2018), CASS (Current Account Switch Service 2013) and Ofcom's text-to-switch (2019) all aim to reduce switching frictions specifically.

The CMA's 2016 retail banking market investigation found switching costs and informational frictions sustained higher prices and weak competition.
items.why: Competition exists on a spectrum shaped by frictions. Policy can target the frictions directly (lower switching costs) rather than only firm conduct.
